The code below simulates sampling 100 individuals with unrelated explanatory (X) and response (Y) variables, conducting linear models, and returning p values for 200 tests. You will need to edit it to set a seed.


```{r, eval=F}

set.seed() ##pick a number to set your seed here

doExp <- function(i){
  myX <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myY <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myModel = lm(myY ~ myX) #fit linear model
  myP = summary(myModel)$coefficients[2,4] #get p value
  return(myP)
}

nTests=200

simulated_pvalues <- sapply(1:nTests, doExp) ## run doExp 1000 times
```

1. a) Calculate the family-wide error rate for an alpha value of 0.05 and 200 tests using the formula from the lecture and the notes.

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
1 - (1-0.05)^200
```

b) Run the simulations in the code above and calculate how many of the simulated p values are below 0.05. How does this compare to your expectation from part a?

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
set.seed(31) ##pick a number to set your seed here

doExp <- function(i){
  myX <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myY <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myModel = lm(myY ~ myX) #fit linear model
  myP = summary(myModel)$coefficients[2,4] #get p value
  return(myP)
}

nTests=200

simulated_pvalues <- sapply(1:nTests, doExp) ## run doExp 1000 times

sum(simulated_pvalues<0.05)
#there were 4 significant results at alpha=0.05, matching my expectation that I would get at least one significant result
```


c) Calculate the appropriate Bonferroni cut-off for 200 tests. How many of the simulated p values are below this cut off?

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}
bonf = 0.05/200
bonf

sum(simulated_pvalues<bonf)
#none
```

d) Use the `p.adjust()` function to calculate an fdr corresponding each simulated p value. What is the lowest fdr? How many fdr valures are below 0.05?

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}
fdrs <- p.adjust(simulated_pvalues, method="fdr") #calculate FDRs

sum(simulated_pvalues<bonf)
```

e) Which method do you think worked best for controlling the family-wise error rate? Why?


2. Edit the code above so that the response variable Y is a function of the explanatory variable X. Pick any `b_0`, but set `b_1 = 2` and set the standard deviation of the residuals to `3`. If you get stuck, check the starter code from the simulation activity from last week. Then, rerun the simulations 200 times to generate a new set of p values.

```{r, eval=F, echo=F}
set.seed(31) ##pick a number to set your seed here
b_0=5
b_1 = 2
mysd = 3

doExp2 <- function(i){
  myX <- runif(100) #sample 100 random numbers
  myY <- b_0+b_1*myX+rnorm(n=100,mean=0,sd=mysd)
  myModel = lm(myY ~ myX) #fit linear model
  myP = summary(myModel)$coefficients[2,4] #get p value
  return(myP)
}

nTests=200

simulated_pvalues2 <- sapply(1:nTests, doExp2) ## run doExp2 200 times
```

a) Make a histogram of the simulated p values and compare to a histogram of the p values from part 1. 

```{r, echo=F,eval=F}
hist(simulated_pvalues)
hist(simulated_pvalues2)

```

b) How many of the simulated p values are below 0.05? Is this more or less than part 1?

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}

sum(simulated_pvalues2<0.05) #more
```

c) How many of the simulated p values are below the Bonferroni cut-off?

```{r, echo=F, eval=F}

sum(simulated_pvalues2<0.05/200) 
```


d) Use the p.adjust() function to calculate an fdr corresponding each simulated p value. What is the lowest fdr? How many fdr valures are below 0.05?


```{r, echo=F, eval=F}
fdrs <- p.adjust(simulated_pvalues2, method="fdr") #calculate FDRs

sum(fdrs<0.05)

min(fdrs)
```


e) Which method do you think worked best for controlling the family-wise error rate? Why?
